title: A Stranger in the Tide
subtitle: The Shore I Choose · Chapter 1 of 10
content:
The first thing I remembered was the sound of water.

Not where I had been before it. Not how I had arrived. Not the faces that might have called me home. Only the endless, patient withdrawal of the tide, taking a thin lace of foam back across dark sand.

I lay on a beach beneath a sky full of unfamiliar stars. My mouth tasted of salt. There was a little brass key tied to my wrist with blue thread, and I knew three things about it: it was mine, it mattered, and I had no idea why.

I sat up too quickly. The shore tilted.

“Whoa, hey! If you're going to collapse in front of a legend, at least give me a dramatic warning. I had a breathtaking rescue planned. There was going to be a pose.”

The voice belonged to a man the size of a very confident mountain. He stood beside an outrigger canoe pulled above the surf, carrying a fishhook nearly as big as I was. Tattoos covered his arms and chest, and one of them appeared to be watching me with a suspicious expression.

I stared. He grinned.

“Yes, the tattoos move. Yes, I'm magnificent. You can ask the important questions in whichever order you like.”

“What beach is this?”

His smile faltered by a fraction.

“Okay. Apparently we're starting with geography.”

“And who are you?”

That brought it back. He spread his arms wide enough to make the rising sun look as though it belonged to him.

“Maui. Demigod, legendary wayfinder, rescuer of the sun, occasional hero to people who forget to send thank-you gifts.”

“I don't think I've ever heard of you.”

The tattoo of a little man on his chest doubled over laughing.

Maui looked offended on principle. “Well. That's a new one.”

I meant to apologize, but something else was happening. The more I searched for my own name, the more the inside of my head felt like a house in which all the doors had been painted over. I could remember the purpose of a spoon, the shape of a storm cloud, and how to tell when somebody was pretending not to worry. I could not remember a single person who had loved me.

“I don't know who I am,” I said.

The words sounded small against the sea.

Maui stopped performing. Not completely; I suspected that would require a natural disaster. But he lowered the hook and sat on a rock several careful steps away.

The tiny tattooed version of him planted both feet on his chest and pointed accusingly at the stretch of beach where he'd been posing. Maui looked down.

"Okay, okay. I see you." He rolled his enormous shoulders and planted the hook in the sand. "Turns out the magnificent rescue of a confused stranger has a second part. Food. Water. Very little dramatic narration."

The tattoo gave him an approving thumbs-up, then gestured frantically toward my trembling hands.

"Right. That too." Maui's grin grew crooked. "For the record, I am exceptionally good at rescuing people. The part after the rescue? Still accepting suggestions."

I laughed once, mostly in surprise. His chest puffed up as if he'd won a contest. But he stayed on the rock instead of closing the distance, and I was glad he knew when the audience was only one frightened person.

“Do you know if you're hurt?”

“I don't think so.”

“Hungry?”

“Yes.”

“Excellent. Two questions answered. We're already making progress.”

He produced a piece of fruit from a bag by the canoe, held it out, and waited until I reached for it. He didn't move closer without permission.

“There's a place inland,” he said, nodding toward a green valley between the cliffs. “Lanterns, a spring, doors that lead places they shouldn't. I've been trying to find out what makes them open. Then I found you. With that.”

He pointed at my wrist.

I touched the brass key. A faint warmth moved through the blue thread.

“Does it tell you who I am?”

“No.” His answer came quickly, without the usual flourish. “And I'm not going to invent an answer just to sound impressive.”

“That must be difficult for you.”

The grin returned. “You have no idea.”

It turned out that standing was not the same thing as walking.

My knees buckled on the first attempt. I caught myself against the side of the canoe, hard enough that the outrigger creaked, and discovered I was frightened of how quickly my body could decide things without consulting me.

Maui held out a hand.

I stared at it.

He waited.

"You're allowed to take it," he said. "You are also allowed to refuse it. I have been told I am very good at holding still when instructed."

"By whom?"

"Several very brave people."

I almost smiled. I took his hand and stood again.

Up close, his tattoos shifted like small shadows across sun-warmed stone. The little tattooed Maui on his chest pointed dramatically toward the inland hills, then tapped his own forehead.

"What's he doing?" I asked.

"Reminding me that I have an excellent brain."

"Is he doing it sarcastically?"

"Of course not."

The little figure rolled his eyes.

I laughed, and the movement made my head hurt. Maui guided me toward a dry stretch of sand and sat down far enough away that I could breathe without feeling watched.

I tried to inventory what I knew. The sea had a pull and a rhythm. The large waves broke farther out, and the beach narrowed where the dark rocks gave way to a line of grass. Someone had placed three small wooden stakes above the tide marks. Their tops were painted white.

"Why are those there?" I asked.

"Water markers. The tide rises high enough in storms that nobody should camp below them."

"Who put them there?"

"Someone who understands the sea and distrusts people who think they can boss it around."

"Do you like them?"

"Mostly."

I looked at the markers again. They were simple things, but the care behind them moved me. Somebody had measured danger and left a warning for a stranger.

Maui followed my gaze.

"I can carry you to the valley if you want."

"Would that be safer?"

"Probably. But you've looked at the path three times, so I suspect you want to walk."

I did. I wanted to know whether my legs would hold and whether I could make my own way between the rocks, even if I needed help.

"I'd like to try."

"Then we'll try."

A gull landed beside the canoe and began investigating the bag of fruit. Maui made a threatening face.

The gull stole a piece anyway.

"Magnificent guardian of the breakfast," I said.

He looked offended.

"I was distracted by a very interesting human."

I waited for him to ask me something personal I couldn't answer.

Instead he pointed at the brass key.

"May I look?"

I unwound the blue thread just enough to hold the key up. He leaned forward but didn't take it.

"Not a hook," he said. "Not a fishing weight. Not something I recognize from my own voyaging."

"Could it belong to the valley?"

"Maybe. That's where we'll ask."

"And if they tell me I have to stay?"

His expression sharpened.

"They'd have to explain themselves to me."

I didn't know whether that was reassuring. He seemed to realize it.

"And to you," he added. "You get a say."

I held the key against my palm.

That was the first thing anyone had said to me that sounded less like a promise to protect me and more like a promise to listen.

We walked toward the trees when I could stand. Maui carried his hook over one shoulder and kept pace with me even when I moved slowly. At the edge of the forest I looked back.

The tide had already erased the shape my body had left in the sand.

For a moment I was terrified that the world would do the same to the rest of me.

Maui seemed to notice. He didn't promise that my memory would return. Instead he pointed out a path where lanterns hung from the branches, each with a different color of flame.

“Come on,” he said. “Let's find out what kind of trouble you like.”

I followed him, because I could make that one decision without remembering anything else.
